The question of whether electric cars are truly "green" yields genuinely conflicting research outcomes and opinions across the retrieved evidence. Sources citing the IEA, ICCT, EPA, and MIT broadly agree that EVs produce lower lifetime greenhouse gas emissions than ICE vehicles [d1][d2][d3][d4][d6], but the degree of benefit varies significantly: in Europe, EVs generate up to 69% less CO2 per kilometre than petrol cars, while in India the figure is only 34%, depending on how electricity is sourced [d6]. On the other hand, a skeptical perspective argues that battery production alone emits between 23,000 and 32,000 pounds of CO2 per battery, and since 63% of U.S. electricity comes from fossil fuels, EVs largely shift emissions from the tailpipe to the power plant rather than eliminating them [d9]. Additional concerns include the environmental costs of mining copper and other materials—EVs use two to three times more copper than petrol vehicles, potentially driving a 300%+ surge in global copper demand by 2050 [d5]—and the argument that even widespread EV adoption will not reduce carbon emissions fast enough to meet climate targets [d10]. In summary, while the mainstream scientific and institutional consensus holds that EVs are better for the environment than conventional vehicles over their lifetime [d1][d3][d4], the extent of their "greenness" is heavily context-dependent, and some sources contest whether they represent a sufficient or genuinely clean solution [d9][d10].
